claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys with uniform compositional homogeneity will resist diffusion-driven atomic segregation during exposure to 700–1000°C in argon better than alloys with pre-existing compositional fluctuations.
Resistance to segregation will allow homogeneous nanoalloys to maintain a stable single-phase structure at 700–1000°C.
Compositional homogeneity will preserve mechanical integrity during high-temperature exposure relative to compositionally heterogeneous samples.
Atomic-scale compositional uniformity governs susceptibility to segregation and secondary-phase formation.
In compositionally non-uniform alloys, thermally activated diffusion promotes further local segregation.
Diffusion-driven local segregation leads to phase separation and microstructural instability.
Compositional homogeneity minimizes atomic diffusion pathways.
Reduced diffusion pathways and chemical-potential gradients delay or suppress high-temperature segregation.
Homogeneous nanoalloys will show significantly less atomic segregation than heterogeneous samples after equivalent thermal treatment.
Homogeneous nanoalloys will form fewer secondary phases than heterogeneous samples after equivalent thermal treatment.
Compositionally heterogeneous nanoalloys exposed to 700–1000°C will develop measurable compositional fluctuations and new phases.
At significantly lower temperatures, diffusion may be insufficient to produce the predicted segregation behavior.
Reactive environments may produce different stability behavior because oxidation or other chemical reactions can occur.
The compositional-uniformity threshold required to suppress segregation is unknown.
The influence of particular elemental combinations on diffusion kinetics remains uncertain.
Comparing initially homogeneous and intentionally segregated samples under the same thermal and atmospheric conditions can test the effect of initial compositional uniformity.
Equivalent segregation, secondary-phase formation, or mechanical degradation in the homogeneous and segregated samples would falsify the proposed stabilizing effect of compositional uniformity.
